summary:
We developed VISHWA, an interactive Earth investigation platform that transforms decades of NASA and partner agency data into discoveries anyone can explore. Drop a pin on a rotating globe, ask “Is my city getting hotter?”, and uncover what is changing, how fast, and how convincing the evidence is.
Travel through Earth’s history, scan entire regions, duel two cities, or discover unexpected “climate twins” through machine learning. Explore 19 environmental variables alongside global temperature, atmospheric CO₂ and polar sea ice.
Behind every discovery is rigorous mathematics. Sen’s slope measures the rate of change, Mann–Kendall and regression tests assess statistical significance, and confidence intervals communicate uncertainty. Seasonal adjustment reveals underlying patterns, serial correlation corrections account for related observations, and false discovery control limits misleading findings across thousands of comparisons. Change point detection identifies sudden shifts, while clustering and backtested forecasting reveal similarities and possible futures. Sourced explanations explore possible causes while clearly distinguishing correlation from causation.
Built for NASA’s Earth System Trend Detective challenge, VISHWA translates this analysis into visual verdicts, seasonal fingerprints and an inspectable evidence locker. It makes planetary change personal and understandable, giving students and the public the tools to investigate their world with scientific confidence.
details:
When you run the program locally, please use the START and STOP files.

We built VISHWA, which stands for Validated Insights on Significant Hydro-climate and Weather Anomalies, to help people investigate how the Earth is changing and understand the evidence behind what they find. It combines NASA data, statistical analysis, machine learning and an interactive globe in one platform. Someone can begin with a question like “Is my city getting hotter?” and work through the historical record, compare nearby regions, examine seasonal changes and inspect the mathematics supporting the result.

The name reflects the approach we took throughout development. “Validated Insights” represents our focus on checking calculations and making the evidence accessible. “Significant” refers to the distinction between a visible change, a large change and a statistically supported trend. “Hydro-climate and Weather Anomalies” brings together the connected environmental systems we investigate, including temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, evaporation, humidity, clouds, radiation and wind. Anomalies help users see how conditions differ from what would normally be expected at that place and time of year.

We designed the platform around the challenge’s four main objectives: identifying suitable Earth science variables, acquiring data for a selected region, visualising a sufficiently long time series and calculating the rate and statistical significance of change. We also explored what users might want to ask next, such as whether neighbouring areas are changing differently, which seasons are driving the trend and whether a model could have anticipated some of the changes.

The target audience in the brief played a major role in our decisions. We considered high school and college students, alongside members of the public with some scientific background. We wanted them to be able to start investigating without already knowing how to interpret a regression output or operate a specialist scientific package.

That is why we kept the front page simple. The globe is the centre of the experience, with straightforward controls for choosing a place, selecting something to investigate and moving through time. A short verdict gives users an understandable first answer. They can open an explanation when they want to know more, rather than being confronted with every calculation immediately.

The Explore option reveals the full depth of the platform. It contains case files, variable sweeps, regional scans, comparisons between locations, world surveys, planetary indicators, ranked trends, historical events, saved investigations and learning tools. These are organised into Place tools, Compare & context and Learn. A student can stay with the basic result, while someone looking for a deeper investigation can follow the same question into the underlying evidence.

The onboarding asks two questions: which places matter to the user, and what they would like to follow. Users can choose up to five places and select interests covering heat, water, clouds, land, wind and ice. These choices shape the variables shown on their main page. They can change their preferences later and choose plain, balanced or technical explanations.

Our main local data source is NASA POWER. We support 19 monthly environmental variables across five groups. The temperature variables include average air temperature, average daily highs and lows, the difference between daytime and nighttime temperatures and surface temperature. Water variables include precipitation, relative humidity, specific humidity and total atmospheric column water vapour. Land variables include evaporation, root zone soil wetness, surface soil wetness and snowfall. We also include sunlight under actual and clear sky conditions, downward infrared radiation, cloud cover, wind speed and surface pressure.

Having these variables together makes it possible to investigate connections across the Earth system. A user asking about warming can also examine whether the same location is becoming drier, whether nights are warming differently from days, or whether changes in clouds and sunlight appear alongside the temperature trend.

Many of the local records extend from 1981 to the last complete year, depending on availability. We also use NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 for global temperature and latitude band comparisons, NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory for the Mauna Loa carbon dioxide record, NSIDC Sea Ice Index for Arctic and Antarctic sea ice extent, and NOAA CPC and NCEI for ENSO, Pacific Decadal Oscillation and North Atlantic Oscillation indices.

We were careful about what these sources represent. NASA POWER includes gridded reanalysis and satellite based products, with nominal source resolutions of approximately 0.5° by 0.625° for MERRA-2 and 1° for radiation products. Selecting a pin therefore means investigating the available grid data around that location. It does not imply a measurement taken at that exact building or street, and nearby locations can share an underlying source cell.

The platform keeps source names, units, periods, coverage and relevant limitations available to the user. We identify model derived products and recognise that changes in their inputs can sometimes resemble environmental shifts. We also avoid blindly averaging different datasets. Products need compatible definitions, units, geographic coverage, time scales and baselines before combining their values would be scientifically meaningful.

Users can explore the Earth by searching for a place, entering coordinates, dropping a pin, rotating the globe or switching to a flat map. The Earth itself is rendered using geographic geometry, shading and atmospheric effects. Its visual appearance is kept separate from the scientific layers, so decorative effects are not mistaken for satellite observations.

For temperature, precipitation and cloud cover, we created a coarse monthly global preview from NASA POWER samples on a 15 degree grid for 2023 to 2025. This gives users something meaningful to explore before choosing a location. It is clearly labelled as an approximate preview and is not used for local trend calculations, significance tests or forecasts.

Once a place is selected, the platform can show more detailed monthly values and anomalies on a small local grid. Users can play or pause the timeline, move one month at a time, scrub to a date and adjust playback speed. Additional details show the source, coverage and grid values. Detailed monthly requests cover up to ten years at a time, while the trend analysis uses the longer available record.

Each investigation produces a case file. Its Overview answers what changed, where, by how much and how strong the evidence is. The Detail view opens the historical record, seasonal patterns, robustness checks, climate context, forecast lab and scientific caveats.

We estimate the rate of change using Sen’s slope, which takes the median of the slopes between pairs of observations. This gives us a robust estimate that is less sensitive to individual extreme values than relying entirely on ordinary least squares. We report the rate per decade, a 95% confidence interval and the estimated total change over the selected period. Percentage change is included where it is physically meaningful.

The Mann Kendall test assesses whether the record contains evidence of a consistent upward or downward trend. Our implementation accounts for tied values, continuity and serial dependence. Ordinary least squares regression provides a complementary slope, standard error, confidence interval, coefficient of determination and regression t test.

Temporal dependence was an important consideration. Climate years often resemble the years around them, so treating every observation as independent can make the evidence appear stronger than it really is. We adjust for positive lag one autocorrelation and use effective degrees of freedom in the regression test.

We also account for the fact that searching many variables and places increases the opportunity to find apparently significant results by chance. Benjamini Hochberg false discovery control is applied across the relevant comparison groups, including variables, regional cells, world sample sites, calendar months and climate indices. The Ledger applies a joint correction across its available findings.

Data completeness is checked before those calculations are made. Annual values require all 12 valid months so that an incomplete year is not biased towards whichever seasons happen to be present. Missing values remain missing, and land specific variables are not invented over oceans. Core trend analysis requires at least 20 complete years. We also handle constant records, heavily tied values and numerical scaling issues.

We distinguish the size of a change from the strength of its evidence. A substantial estimated change can still be uncertain, while a smaller change can be detectable in a long and consistent record. Comparing the estimated change with normal annual variability helps users understand how clearly it stands out from the fluctuations usually experienced at that location.

The evidence locker brings together five visible checks: whether the principal trend test supports the result, whether regression agrees, whether most usable calendar months move in the same direction, whether the trend survives changes to the record’s endpoints and whether the estimated change stands out from normal variability. The evidence grade is a transparent assessment rubric rather than a probability that a conclusion is true.

Users can inspect an evidence trace generated by the backend. It shows data completeness, calculation methods, corrections, numerical results and caveats. The plain language verdict and the technical explanation use the same computed analysis. This also keeps optional language models separate from the calculations that determine slopes, p values and scientific verdicts.

We built several ways to examine the same record. Annual charts show the long term behaviour, while monthly anomalies remove the usual seasonal cycle. A complete 12 month rolling anomaly average helps reveal broader movement. Climate stripes provide a compact visual history, and a radial seasonal fingerprint shows which months contribute most strongly to the trend.

The emergence chart asks how the evidence changes as more observations become available. It repeatedly analyses progressively longer sections of the record and identifies the beginning of the final sustained period of significant evidence. This helps users understand why a short record can be inconclusive even when a longer record reveals a clearer pattern.

We also check whether a straight line is a reasonable description of the data. A comparison between gradual and step shaped change, together with the Pettitt change point test, helps identify abrupt shifts. For sufficiently long records, we remove five years from the beginning, the end and both ends to see how sensitive the result is to the selected period.

Sweep lets users examine every available variable at one place. It ranks the findings and corrects for the multiple tests. This makes discovery part of the experience: someone arriving with a temperature question might find that the clearest evidence at their location involves sunlight, humidity or nighttime conditions.

Scan a region extends the investigation across a geographic grid. It shows individual cell results, corrected evidence, the strongest increases and decreases, and a regional composite weighted by the area represented at each latitude. It highlights opposing local trends that could disappear inside an average. Grid construction also handles longitude wrapping and avoids duplicate coordinates near the poles.

Scan includes Moran’s I to investigate whether similar trends cluster geographically. A seeded permutation test repeatedly rearranges the values across the grid to assess how unusual the observed spatial pattern is. This gives users a statistical way to examine a pattern they notice on the map.

Duel compares two locations through their case files, records and estimated rates of change. A Welch Satterthwaite comparison of regression slopes provides a difference estimate, uncertainty interval and statistical assessment. Users can investigate questions such as whether two regions show distinguishable warming rates, with the approximation of independence between locations documented.

Some Explore tools can be opened together. Users can compare two places while scanning the surrounding region, or examine a case file alongside its regional results. Shared location state keeps the investigations aligned. The views sit alongside each other on larger screens and stack on smaller devices.

World examines a selected variable across 68 sample locations. Marker properties communicate trend direction, change relative to normal variability and whether the finding survives correction across the sites. Annual records support historical playback. We identify these as sample locations rather than presenting them as a complete global measurement field.

Planet Vitals connects those regional findings with global temperature, Mauna Loa carbon dioxide and Arctic and Antarctic sea ice. These four indicators use the case file analysis engine. ENSO, PDO and NAO are shown as climate rhythms, keeping their oscillatory behaviour distinct from the long term trends being investigated.

The Ledger brings together over a thousand available combinations of variables and sample sites, alongside the planetary trend indicators. Users can filter and rank findings by statistical evidence, magnitude or change relative to normal variability. Relevant results can include sourced context about possible explanations.

The suspect lineup examines how local variability moves with ENSO, PDO and NAO. It uses detrended correlations, effective sample sizes and correction across the indices. An ENSO adjusted analysis uses partial regression to separate shared temporal drift from the estimated association with ENSO.

For temperature, we also provide a local amplification measure and a comparison with the relevant GISTEMP latitude band. This gives an independently sourced regional reference while keeping its broader geographic scale clear.

An exploratory ridge regression model investigates how useful the climate indices are for explaining annual variability. It uses leave one year out validation, cross validated performance and permutation importance. These results describe associations and predictive relationships; they do not establish a cause or constitute an operational forecast.

One of the most unusual parts of VISHWA is its climate twins feature. We give each sample location a fingerprint describing how 15 broadly available variables are changing relative to their normal variability. We weight the variable groups so that several temperature measures cannot overwhelm the other environmental dimensions.

K means clustering, initialised with k means++, groups places with similar fingerprints. Silhouette scores show how clearly the groups are separated, while bootstrap resampling and the adjusted Rand index assess their stability. Users can explore different numbers of groups. Cosine similarity identifies the closest climate twins, including places that may be geographically far apart.

These twins share patterns of change rather than necessarily having the same climate. We report weak separation or unstable groupings so that an interesting visual result is not automatically presented as a strong scientific classification.

The annual Forecast Lab compares eight approaches: repeating the previous year, using the long term mean, a linear trend, a Theil Sen trend, damped trend smoothing, a trend with autoregressive persistence, ridge regression using previous years and time, and an ensemble.

Rolling origin backtests evaluate predictions at horizons of one to five years using the historical information available at each starting point. The lab reports mean absolute error, performance by horizon and improvement over simple baselines. Split conformal prediction intervals use historical forecast errors, and a separate chronological procedure assesses interval coverage.

A replay slider lets users explore earlier predictions alongside what happened afterwards. Its uncertainty bands are labelled as an illustration using present day calibration, keeping the replay distinct from the performance assessment. When the models do not demonstrate sufficient improvement over a baseline, the interface communicates that lack of skill.

We built a separate monthly forecast for temperature, precipitation and cloud cover over one to three months. Its five candidates include a seasonal baseline, harmonic seasonality with a damped trend, regularised seasonal autoregression, a seasonal trend with persistent residuals and an ensemble.

The monthly workflow requires at least 120 contiguous observations and checks completeness, improvement over the baseline at the requested horizons and prediction interval coverage. Grid cells are aligned to a common final observed month. Forecasts are withheld when the eligibility checks fail.

Eligible predictions can extend the globe timeline, with labels, hatching and a clear boundary between observations and forecasts. Users can inspect the training period, model scores and calibration performance. We recognise the uncertainty remaining in model selection and short climate records, so these outputs are described as statistical outlooks rather than physical climate projections or predictions of individual weather events.

The “Why might this be happening?” option connects measured findings with published scientific context. A curated explanation path works without an external language model. An optional OpenAI Responses API integration can extend explanations through restricted scientific search domains and citation provenance checks.

The explanation service uses facts computed by the backend and cannot change the statistical result. We distinguish measured findings from physical mechanisms and plausible local explanations. A correlation, a model’s feature importance or a relevant publication is not treated as proof that one mechanism caused the observed trend.

The Events tool connects 15 documented environmental events with investigations of the relevant location and period. It checks what the chosen record actually shows, including when coarse monthly data do not clearly capture a memorable heat wave, drought or flood.

Eleven guided investigations introduce questions involving Arctic warming, sunlight near Delhi, Amazon rainfall, nighttime warming and forecast performance. Ask interprets supported questions through transparent keyword and geographic matching, including locations, coordinates, variables and years.

Learn brings together the guided cases, glossary, curated Explainer and source information. Users can open scientific terms directly from the interface, and the Explainer can use the current case’s values to connect a definition with the investigation in front of them. Ask and the built in Explainer remain separate from the optional AI service.

The globe also includes approximate capital locations for all 193 UN member states. Capital overviews provide coordinates, solar time, distance from the equator and selected geographic facts. A GDELT integration can add environmental news context.

We made news requests gradual and bounded, and designed callouts to avoid each other and the main controls. They pause during interaction and have keyboard accessible alternatives. Publisher status and attention labels are explicit. These labels do not imply independent verification of an article or an official warning, and news remains separate from the scientific evidence.

An optional Meteomatics adapter provides current and short range hourly temperature, precipitation, cloud cover and wind information. Operational weather, NASA climate history and VISHWA’s own forecasts retain separate labels and provenance. The credentialed OpenAI and Meteomatics paths have been exercised using simulated responses; live credential checks remain a separate verification step.

Users can save labelled and coloured pins containing the location, variable, period and available scan information. Pin history supports undo, and cached results help restore earlier investigations. Shareable links preserve question state, while browser Back and Forward navigation remains consistent.

The expandable chart viewer provides exact value readouts, adjustable ranges, appropriate display unit conversions and linear or logarithmic scales where valid. It explains when a logarithmic view cannot represent the values. PNG and CSV exports make the results useful for lessons, presentations and further analysis.

Profiles are stored locally on the device. Users can edit interests and places, reorder locations, change detail preferences, import or export a profile, reset it and sign out. The sign in experience is explicitly a demonstration rather than secure online authentication. Passwords are discarded without being stored or transmitted, and the display identity uses a masked email.

Accessibility influenced the interface through keyboard navigation, descriptive labels, visible focus, focus handling in dialogs, reduced motion preferences and responsive layouts. Colour is supported by symbols, text, line styles and hatching. Mobile controls become a bottom sheet so that the Earth remains visible. We implemented these supports while recognising that full accessibility certification would require further testing.

We reviewed the wider challenge resource ecosystem, including Giovanni, Hydrology Time Series, AppEEARS, NOAA Climate Data Online, KNMI Climate Explorer, SeaWiFS research examples and Canadian radar, water mission and geospatial resources. We distinguished integrated sources from reference material and possible extensions. Authentication, licensing, processing requirements and reliability informed our scope.

The backend uses Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn and HTTPX. The frontend uses React, JavaScript, Vite, HTML and CSS, with a custom canvas globe and SVG charts. Geographic processing uses D3 Geo, TopoJSON Client and World Atlas, with Natural Earth geometry supporting the map.

We implemented the statistics and machine learning directly in Python, keeping the calculations inspectable and avoiding a dependency on external language models for numerical inference. The core application does not require a dedicated GPU. Development used Git, automated Python and JavaScript tests, production builds and documented browser walkthroughs, with disclosed assistance from Claude, Gemini and visual design assistance from Fable.

We checked core statistical results against SciPy, pymannkendall, pyhomogeneity and established Sen interval conventions, preserving reference outputs as regression tests. We also used simulations to investigate false alarm behaviour under persistence. In one documented scenario with 44 annual observations and strong serial dependence, the unadjusted method produced approximately 38.5% false alarms, compared with approximately 6.6% after adjustment at a nominal 5% level. This describes that specific simulation rather than a universal accuracy claim.

Reliability work includes bounded caches, concurrency controls, timeouts, response size limits, request cancellation, rate limits and appropriate retries. Expensive monthly backtests run away from the server’s main event loop. Optional service failures produce explicit unavailable, stale, fallback or withheld states rather than fabricated information.

Credentials remain in server configuration. Explanation requests use signed case identifiers and server verified facts, while health reporting avoids exposing secrets. Windows launch tools, stale server detection and version warnings help prevent accidental use of older builds. Production serving and deployment configurations are prepared, with successful public deployment treated as a separate operational milestone.

We want VISHWA to help users ask better questions about environmental change and understand how scientific answers are built. A student can investigate home, a teacher can develop a lesson around a guided case, and a curious user can compare a local finding with another part of the world. The simple front page gives them somewhere to begin, while Explore lets that same question grow into a regional investigation, a seasonal fingerprint, a climate twin search, a forecast experiment and a mathematical evidence trail they can examine for themselves.
